meta.about: Fact checks of the bank's clues against sources, by pipeline/fact-check.ts. See lib/questions/clueEval/factCheck.ts.

checks.text: This future president is the only one ever to hold a U.S. patent, granted in 1849 for a device to lift boats over shallow water.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: 'the only United States president to be a patentee'; Patent No. 6,469, 'Buoying Vessels Over Shoals', granted 22 May 1849, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Lincoln%27s_patent

checks.text: A skilled wrestler in his youth and, at 6 foot 4, the tallest ever to hold his office, he had almost no formal schooling.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: Lincoln at 6 ft 4 in is the tallest president, ahead of LBJ at about 6 ft 3.5 in, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heights_of_presidents_and_presidential_candidates_of_the_United_States ; he won a noted wrestling match and had less than 12 months of formal schooling, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Lincoln

checks.text: The first Republican elected president, he was born in a one-room log cabin in Kentucky.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: won in 1860, 'becoming the first Republican president'; born in 'a one-room log cabin' in Kentucky, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Lincoln

checks.text: This bearded 16th U.S. president, honored on the penny and the five-dollar bill, was assassinated in 1865.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: his portrait appears on the penny and the $5 bill; shot by Booth on 14 April 1865, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Lincoln

checks.text: In parts of the American South, this body feature goes by the folk name 'goozle'.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: 'In the American South, goozle is used colloquially to describe the laryngeal prominence,' citing the Dictionary of Smoky Mountain English. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam%27s_apple

checks.text: Textbooks say the two cartilage plates that form this feature meet at about 90 degrees in men but about 120 degrees in women.
checks.evidence: Kenhub: in females the thyroid laminae 'meet at an angle of approximately 120 degrees'; in males the angle is 'more acute at around 90 degrees.' https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/thyroid-cartilage

checks.text: Surgeons can shrink this feature with a chondrolaryngoplasty, an operation colloquially called a 'tracheal shave'.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: it can be surgically reduced by 'chondrolaryngoplasty, or colloquially as a tracheal shave.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam%27s_apple

checks.text: This throat bump is traditionally said to be named for a legend, found nowhere in the Bible, that forbidden fruit stuck in the first man's throat.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: the common belief was that a piece of the fatal apple stuck in Adam's throat; 'The story is not found in the Bible or other Jewish, Christian, or Islamic writings.' The clue's 'traditionally said' covers the rival mistranslation theory. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam%27s_apple

checks.text: This is the only continent crossed by both the equator and the prime meridian.
checks.evidence: Geography Realm: Africa is the only continent with land on both the equator and the prime meridian. https://www.geographyrealm.com/continent-lies-four-hemispheres/

checks.text: This continent has the world's youngest population, with a median age under 20.
checks.evidence: Worldometer gives Africa a median age of 19.5; Intelpoint (from Worldometer data) says Africa, at about 19, has the youngest population of any continent. https://www.worldometers.info/world-population/africa-population/ and https://intelpoint.co/insights/with-a-median-age-of-19-years-africa-has-the-youngest-population-while-europe-has-the-oldest-population-43-years/

checks.text: This continent has 54 countries, more than any other.
checks.evidence: WorldAtlas: Africa has 54 countries, the most of any continent, ahead of Asia (48) and Europe (44). https://www.worldatlas.com/geography/continents-by-number-of-countries.html

checks.text: Home to the Serengeti's lions and elephants, this continent lies south of Europe across the Mediterranean.
checks.evidence: Africa lies south of Europe across the Mediterranean and contains the Serengeti. https://www.geographyrealm.com/continent-lies-four-hemispheres/

checks.text: This tale was never translated from an Arabic original; Hanna Diyab, a storyteller from Aleppo, told it to the French translator Antoine Galland in Paris in 1709.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: Galland met Hanna, who had travelled from Aleppo to Paris, in March 1709; Hanna Diyab article lists Aladdin as told on 5 May 1709, apparently from oral telling; 'any authentic Arabic textual source has not been found' and the Chavis and Sabbagh Arabic manuscripts are back-translations of Galland's French. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aladdin https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanna_Diyab

checks.text: The first printed version of this tale, from 1710, is set in 'one of the cities of China', and its hero commands two genies, the weaker one bound to a magic ring.
checks.evidence: Aladdin article: set in 'one of the cities of China'; ring genie 'too weak to directly undo any of the magic of the genie of the lamp'; volumes ix and x 'published in 1710'. Editions list: 'Vols. 9, 10 = 1712, Paris: Florentin Delaulne.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aladdin https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_Mille_et_Une_Nuits
checks.problem: The 1710 date is disputed: Wikipedia's Aladdin article says volumes IX and X appeared in 1710, but its Les Mille et Une Nuits editions list dates volumes 9 and 10 to 1712 (Paris, Florentin Delaulne). The setting and the weaker ring genie are correct.
checks.fix: The first printed version of this tale, in Antoine Galland's French Nights, is set in 'one of the cities of China', and its hero commands two genies, the weaker one bound to a magic ring.

checks.text: In British Christmas pantomimes of this story, the hero's mother is the comic dame Widow Twankey, named after a cheap brand of Chinese tea.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: Widow Twankey, Aladdin's mother in pantomime, was 'named after a cheap brand of China tea' (twankay, an inferior green tea); first used in H. J. Byron's 1861 Aladdin. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Widow_Twankey

checks.text: Robin Williams voiced the wisecracking Genie in Disney's 1992 animated film of this tale, whose street-urchin hero falls for Princess Jasmine.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: Robin Williams voiced the Genie in the 1992 film; Aladdin is 'an Arabian street urchin' in love with Princess Jasmine. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aladdin_(1992_Disney_film)

checks.text: The first printed version of this tale is set not in Arabia but in 'one of the cities of China', where its hero is a penniless ne'er-do-well whose late father was a tailor.
checks.evidence: Galland's French text opens 'Sire, dans la capitale d'un royaume de la Chine, très riche et d'une vaste étendue... il y avoit un tailleur nommé Mustafa', 'Mustafa le tailleur étoit fort pauvre', and the son 'étoit méchant, opiniâtre, désobéissant' https://archive.org/stream/lesmilleunenuits08gall/lesmilleunenuits08gall_djvu.txt ; Wikipedia credits Galland with the first printing and gives Burton's 'impoverished young ne'er-do-well' in 'one of the cities of Ancient China', with his late father Mustapha a tailor https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aladdin
checks.problem: The quoted phrase 'one of the cities of China' is Burton's 1885 wording, not the first printed version's. Galland's 1710s French text opens 'dans la capitale d'un royaume de la Chine' (in the capital of a kingdom of China). The China setting, the poor tailor father and the unruly son all check out.
checks.fix: The first printed version of this tale is set not in Arabia but in the capital of a kingdom of China, where its hero is an unruly ne'er-do-well whose late father was a poor tailor.

checks.text: This tale has no known Arabic original; like Ali Baba, it was told to the French translator Antoine Galland in Paris in 1709 by Hanna Diyab, a storyteller from Aleppo.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia's Aladdin article says the tale 'was not part of the original Nights manuscripts and any authentic Arabic textual source has not been found'. It says the Chavis and Sabbagh Arabic manuscripts were shown by Muhsin Mahdi to be back-translations of Galland's French. It calls Hanna Diyab 'a Maronite storyteller from Aleppo' whom Galland met in Paris in 1709. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aladdin ; Wikipedia's Hanna Diyab article lists the tales Diyab told Galland in Paris in 1709: Aladdin on May 5 and Ali Baba on May 27. It also says Diyab was born in Aleppo. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanna_Diyab

checks.text: In British Christmas pantomimes of this story, the hero's mother is a comic dame named after a cheap brand of Chinese tea.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia says Widow Twankey, a pantomime dame played by an older man, 'was named after a cheap brand of China tea', an inferior grade of green tea. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Widow_Twankey ; the Aladdin article says 'the traditional Aladdin pantomime is the source of the well-known pantomime character Widow Twankey (Aladdin's mother)'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aladdin

checks.text: In British Christmas pantomimes of this story, the hero's mother is a comic dame whose name comes from a cheap Chinese green tea.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia says Widow Twankey is the pantomime dame in this story, a comic female role usually played by a man, and that she 'was named after a cheap brand of China tea'. It adds that 'Twankay' is an inferior grade of green tea named after Tunxi in Anhui (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Widow_Twankey). Merriam-Webster defines Twankay tea as 'a green tea of inferior quality' (https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/twankay). Sixth Tone says that in 1861 H.J. Byron named the hero's mother 'Widow Twankey' after the lower-grade Tunxi green tea, and that she became a pantomime dame played by a man in drag, https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018829

checks.text: This physicist was offered the presidency of Israel in 1952 and declined, saying he lacked the aptitude and experience to deal properly with people.
checks.evidence: Offer made 17 November 1952; he declined: 'I lack both the natural aptitude and the experience to deal properly with people.' https://www.jewishvirtuallibrary.org/offering-the-presidency-of-israel-to-albert-einstein

checks.text: After this physicist died in 1955, the pathologist who did the autopsy removed his brain without permission and kept it for decades.
checks.evidence: 'No permission for the removal and preservation had been given by Einstein or his family'; Harvey kept the brain about 43 years, to 1998. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Stoltz_Harvey

checks.text: This physicist's most famous theory never won him a Nobel Prize — the award instead cited his work on the photoelectric effect.
checks.evidence: The 1921 prize cited services to theoretical physics and especially the law of the photoelectric effect; relativity was not mentioned and he never won for it. https://content.time.com/time/specials/packages/article/0,28804,1936731_1936743_1936804,00.html

checks.text: This physicist, known for E=mc² and a mane of wild white hair, has a surname that is now shorthand for 'genius.'
checks.evidence: E=mc2, his hair and 'Einstein' as a byword for genius are common knowledge; Nobel context from https://content.time.com/time/specials/packages/article/0,28804,1936731_1936743_1936804,00.html

checks.text: This ruler's funeral cart was hijacked on its way to Macedonia by his general Ptolemy, who took the body to Egypt, where Augustus later came to see it.
checks.evidence: History Hit says the funeral cart left Babylon for Aegae in Macedonia, Ptolemy seized it and took the body to Egypt, and Augustus later visited the body. https://www.historyhit.com/alexander-corpse/

checks.text: After this ruler defeated King Porus in India, his exhausted army refused to march past the Hyphasis River and forced him to turn back.
checks.evidence: History Skills says he defeated Porus at the Hydaspes, and at the Hyphasis his exhausted army, with Coenus as spokesman, refused to go on, so he turned back. https://historyskills.com/classroom/ancient-history/hyphasis-mutiny

checks.text: This ruler named a city after his horse Bucephalus, which he had tamed as a boy when no one else could.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia says he founded the city Bucephala in honour of the horse, and won it at twelve or thirteen by taming it when no one else could. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bucephalus

checks.text: Legend says this undefeated conqueror wept because there were no more worlds left for him to conquer.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia's lead says he was 'undefeated in battle'. The weeping story is a popular legend (Plutarch's version differs), and the clue presents it as 'Legend says'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_the_Great

checks.text: This metal's modern smelting method was found independently in 1886 by the American Charles Martin Hall and the Frenchman Paul Héroult, who were both born in 1863 and both died in 1914.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: the process was found independently in 1886 by Hall and Heroult; Heroult was born 10 April 1863 and died 9 May 1914; Hall was born December 6, 1863 and died December 27, 1914. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_H%C3%A9roult https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Martin_Hall

checks.text: Before it capped the Washington Monument in 1884, a 100-ounce pyramid of this metal, then about as valuable as silver, was shown at Tiffany's in New York, where visitors stepped over it.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: the 100-ounce aluminum apex, made of a metal then 'as rare and valuable as silver', was shown at Tiffany's in New York, where visitors stepped over it, before being set in place on December 6, 1884. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Monument

checks.text: Napoleon III reportedly saved his dinner plates made of this metal, then a costly novelty, for his most honored guests.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: Napoleon III 'reserved his few sets of aluminium dinner plates and eating utensils for his most honored guests', a report the clue hedges with 'reportedly'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hall%E2%80%93H%C3%A9roult_process

checks.text: This lightweight metal, the most abundant in Earth's crust, goes into soda cans and kitchen foil, and in Britain its name has an extra 'i'.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: 'In the Earth's crust, aluminium is the most abundant metallic element'; 'aluminium' is the British/IUPAC spelling and 'aluminum' the North American one; cans and foil are standard uses. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium

checks.text: This metal's oxide, corundum, forms both rubies and sapphires, colored red by traces of chromium or blue by iron and titanium.
checks.evidence: Corundum is 'a crystalline form of aluminium oxide (Al2O3)'; 'Rubies are red due to the presence of chromium' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corundum ; GIA: 'When the trace elements are iron and titanium, the corundum is blue sapphire'; 'Chromium can cause the red color of ruby' https://www.gia.edu/sapphire-description

checks.text: This company's founder considered calling it 'Relentless', and that web address still leads to its site.
checks.evidence: Bezos registered Relentless.com as a possible name; fetching relentless.com today returns a 302 redirect to www.amazon.com. https://mentalfloss.com/article/654621/why-relentless-redirects-amazon and https://relentless.com

checks.text: This company's founder quit a New York hedge-fund job and drafted its business plan on a cross-country drive to Seattle.
checks.evidence: Bezos left his VP job at D. E. Shaw, a Wall Street firm, in 1994; he and MacKenzie drafted the business plan on their road trip to Seattle (some accounts say the drive began in Fort Worth after a flight from New York, but it was still a cross-country drive). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Amazon and https://thinkers50.com/biographies/jeff-bezos/

checks.text: This company's smiling logo is an arrow from A to Z, hinting that it sells everything.
checks.evidence: Cited Fabrik page loaded only a listing. Logotyp.us: the orange arrow runs from the 'a' to the 'z,' suggesting Amazon offers everything from A to Z, and its curve forms a smile. https://logotyp.us/logo/amazon/

checks.text: This e-commerce giant sells nearly everything online and runs the voice assistant Alexa.
checks.evidence: Alexa is a virtual assistant marketed by Amazon. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Alexa

checks.text: This forest gets about 22,000 tons of phosphorus a year from Saharan dust blown across the Atlantic, roughly what rain and floods wash out of it.
checks.evidence: NASA SVS: Saharan dust delivers about 22,000 tons of phosphorus a year, 'about the same amount as that lost from rain and flooding.' https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/11775

checks.text: Patches of unusually fertile black soil in this forest, called terra preta, were made by farming communities between about 450 BCE and 950 CE.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: 'Terra preta soils were created by the pre-Columbian farming communities between 450 BCE and 950 CE.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terra_preta

checks.text: This forest spreads across nine countries, though about 60% of it lies in Brazil.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: the region includes territory of nine nations; 'The majority of the forest, 60%, is in Brazil.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_rainforest

checks.text: This immense South American rainforest, home to jaguars and poison dart frogs, is the biggest on the planet.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: it is the largest tract of tropical rainforest in the world; jaguars and poison dart frogs live there. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_rainforest

checks.text: In 2015 a palaeontologist at a market in Myitkyina, Myanmar, spotted a 99-million-year-old feathered dinosaur tail in a lump of this, which had been taken for a plant.
checks.evidence: Asian Scientist: Xing Lida found the piece in 2015 at an amber market in Myitkyina, Myanmar. It had been seen as 'some kind of plant inclusion,' was about 99 million years old and held a feathered dinosaur tail. https://www.asianscientist.com/2016/12/in-the-lab/feathered-dinosaur-tail-preserved-amber/

checks.text: This material's ancient Greek name, ēlektron, gave us the word 'electricity', because rubbing it makes it attract light things such as bits of paper.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: 'electricity' comes from Latin electrum, from Greek elektron, 'amber.' The page describes rubbed amber attracting 'light bodies,' with bits of paper as an example. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etymology_of_electricity

checks.text: Prussia's king gave Peter the Great a room paneled in this in 1716; called the 'Eighth Wonder of the World', it was looted by the Nazis in 1941 and never found.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: Frederick William I of Prussia presented the room to Peter the Great in 1716. It was dubbed the 'Eighth Wonder of the World.' Army Group North dismantled it in 1941 and took it to Konigsberg. It 'was never seen in public again,' and apart from one mosaic panel it has never been recovered. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amber_Room

checks.text: In 'Jurassic Park', scientists clone dinosaurs from blood inside a mosquito preserved in this golden fossilized tree resin.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: in Crichton's novel and the 1993 film, scientists 'extract the preserved blood of dinosaurs from prehistoric mosquitoes trapped in amber' and clone the dinosaurs. Amber is fossilized tree resin. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amber

checks.text: Russia's Kaliningrad region holds an estimated 90 percent of the world's known deposits of this material, mined on its Baltic coast at Yantarny.
checks.evidence: 'The region around the combine holds 90% of the world's extractable amber'; the combine is Russia's only official amber mine, located in Yantarny, Kaliningrad Oblast https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaliningrad_Amber_Combine

checks.text: In 1933 this American woman launched her own clothing line, with some designs made from parachute silk.
checks.evidence: She launched 'Amelia Fashions' in 1933; some designs used parachute silk and airplane-wing fabric. https://airandspace.si.edu/stories/editorial/amelia-earhart-using-fashion-inspire-flight

checks.text: This flier was the first president of the Ninety-Nines, an organization of women pilots founded in 1929.
checks.evidence: The Ninety-Nines was founded 2 November 1929; Earhart was elected its first president in 1931. https://ninety-nines.org/history/

checks.text: After flying across the Atlantic as a passenger in 1928, she said she had been 'just baggage, like a sack of potatoes.'
checks.evidence: After the 1928 Friendship flight: 'Bill (Wilmer Stultz) did all the flying—had to. I was just baggage, like a sack of potatoes.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amelia_Earhart

checks.text: This pioneering American aviator remains one of history's most famous missing persons.
checks.evidence: American aviation pioneer who disappeared in 1937 and was never found. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amelia_Earhart

checks.text: One judge dismissed this painting as a 'comic valentine', yet it won a bronze medal and a $300 prize at the Art Institute of Chicago's 1930 exhibition.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: one judge called it a 'comic valentine', but a patron persuaded the jury to award the bronze medal and a $300 prize; Mental Floss places it at the 1930 AIC annual exhibition. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Gothic

checks.text: Many Iowans took this painting as an insult when it appeared, and one farm wife was so enraged that she threatened to bite the artist's ear off.
checks.evidence: Mental Floss: 'One farm wife was so enraged by the painting that she threatened to bite Wood's ear off'; Wikipedia covers Iowans' fury. https://www.mentalfloss.com/art/15-things-you-might-not-know-about-american-gothic

checks.text: The man in this painting was modeled on the artist's dentist and the woman on his sister, who insisted the pair were father and daughter, not husband and wife.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: the dentist Byron McKeeby and the sister Nan modeled; Nan said the pair were father and daughter, not husband and wife (Wood confirmed it in a 1941 letter). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Gothic

checks.text: This 1930 Grant Wood painting shows a stern farmer gripping a pitchfork beside a woman, in front of a white farmhouse with a pointed church-style window.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: 1930 painting, Carpenter Gothic house with a Gothic-style window. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Gothic

checks.text: This city's Royal Palace, built in the 1600s as its town hall, rests on 13,659 wooden piles sunk into former swampland.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: built from 1648 as the city hall, it 'was built on 13,659 wooden piles.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Palace_of_Amsterdam

checks.text: Some of this city's narrow canal houses were built leaning slightly forward, so goods hoisted from a beam at the top won't scrape the front.
checks.evidence: 'some houses were even built with a slight forward lean' so hoisted goods would not scrape the facade. https://thedutchdaily.nl/amsterdams-hoisting-hooks-a-history-of-practical-ingenuity/

checks.text: Although it is the national capital, this city does not host its country's government or parliament, which sit in The Hague.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: 'Although Amsterdam is the official capital of the Netherlands, it is not the seat of government'; government institutions are in The Hague. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam

checks.text: The Anne Frank House and the Van Gogh Museum draw crowds to this Dutch city, famed for its canals and bicycles.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia lists the Anne Frank House and Van Gogh Museum among main attractions, with over 100 km of canals and cycling central to the city. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam

checks.text: On a 1923 photo of this spiral, Edwin Hubble crossed out an 'N' for a supposed nova and wrote 'VAR!', having found a variable star that proved it lay outside the Milky Way.
checks.evidence: Carnegie: plate of Oct 5-6, 1923; the star's N is crossed out and marked 'VAR!'; the Cepheid established M31 as separate from our galaxy. https://carnegiescience.edu/about/history/archives/plate-archives/m31var

checks.text: Around 964 CE the astronomer Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi described this object as a 'small cloud' in his Book of Fixed Stars.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: al-Sufi described it c. 964 in his Book of Fixed Stars as a 'small cloud'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andromeda_Galaxy

checks.text: About 2.5 million light-years away, this spiral is, under most viewing conditions, one of the most distant things a person can see with the naked eye.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: about 2.5 million light-years; 'Under most viewing conditions ... one of the most distant objects that can be seen with the naked eye'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andromeda_Galaxy

checks.text: Charles Messier listed this spiral as number 31, and it is heading toward the Milky Way at about 110 km per second, with roughly even odds of a collision within 10 billion years.
checks.evidence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andromeda_Galaxy ; https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/milky-way-andromeda-galaxy-collision-odds ; https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.22863
checks.problem: The 'roughly even odds within 10 billion years' figure is from one 2025 study (Sawala et al.). Wikipedia itself adds that other calculations differ, and an April 2026 Peking University analysis put the merger probability near 90%. The odds are disputed, so stating one figure as fact is too firm. Messier 31 and ~110 km/s are supported.
checks.fix: Charles Messier listed this spiral as number 31, and it is heading toward the Milky Way at about 110 km per second, though astronomers disagree on how likely a collision is.

checks.text: Unlike most temples of its region, this temple faces west, which some scholars link to a funerary role for its builder, King Suryavarman II.
checks.evidence: New World Encyclopedia: 'Unlike most Khmer temples, Angkor Wat is oriented to the west'; Glaize and Coedès conclude Suryavarman intended it as his funerary temple. https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Angkor_Wat

checks.text: Raised in the 12th century as a Hindu temple, it was later embraced by Buddhists who still worship there.
checks.evidence: New World Encyclopedia: built in the 12th century as a temple to Vishnu, later converted to Theravada Buddhist use. https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Angkor_Wat

checks.text: The largest religious structure ever built, this temple appears on its country's national flag.
checks.evidence: Guinness: 'largest religious structure ever built', 162.6 ha. New World Encyclopedia: Angkor Wat appears on every Cambodian national flag. https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/largest-religious-structure

checks.text: This vast temple complex just north of Siem Reap is the most famous monument of Cambodia's ancient Khmer Empire.
checks.evidence: New World Encyclopedia: 'located 5.5 km north of the modern town of Siem Reap', the prime example of Khmer architecture. https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Angkor_Wat

checks.text: This novel's author modeled her heroine's face on a magazine photo of Evelyn Nesbit, the model whose husband shot the architect Stanford White in 1906.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: Montgomery clipped Nesbit's photo from the Metropolitan Magazine as the model for Anne's face; Nesbit's husband Harry Kendall Thaw shot the architect Stanford White on 25 June 1906. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evelyn_Nesbit

checks.text: This novel has been on Japan's national school curriculum since 1952, though its Japanese translator had wanted to call it 'The Girl Gazing Out the Window'.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia says the novel has been on Japan's national school curriculum since 1952; the Anne manuscript site says translator Hanako Muraoka's original title idea was 'The Girl Gazing Out the Window', changed to Akage no An. https://annemanuscript.ca/stories/anne-in-japan

checks.text: In 2014 Guinness World Records named a musical of this book, first staged in Charlottetown in 1965, the world's longest-running annual musical theatre production.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: in March 2014 Guinness World Records recognised the musical, premiered at the Charlottetown Festival in 1965, as the longest-running annual musical theatre production; the Guinness page lists the record. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_of_Green_Gables:_The_Musical

checks.text: This 1908 L. M. Montgomery novel follows a talkative red-haired orphan sent by mistake to a Prince Edward Island farm whose owners wanted a boy.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: published 13 June 1908; Marilla and Matthew wanted a boy from the orphanage, but through a misunderstanding Anne is sent instead. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anne_of_Green_Gables

checks.text: This continent has no native land mammals, and its largest animal that lives only on land is a wingless midge a few millimeters long.
checks.evidence: The largest permanent land animal is the wingless Antarctic midge Belgica antarctica, about 2-6 mm long. https://www.discoverwildlife.com/wildlife/insects-invertebrates/antarctica-insects

checks.text: Its ice sheet is nearly 5 kilometers thick at its deepest and holds well over half of the world's fresh water.
checks.evidence: Maximum thickness about 4.9 km at the Astrolabe Subglacial Basin; holds roughly 61% of all fresh water on Earth. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctic_ice_sheet

checks.text: Under a 1959 treaty no nation may stake a new claim to it, and it has no permanent residents — only rotating crews of scientists.
checks.evidence: Treaty prohibits new territorial claims; the continent has no permanent population (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctic_Treaty_System). Population sources describe temporary residents as scientists plus support staff (engineers, medics, chefs, pilots, logistics). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctic_Treaty_System
checks.problem: The treaty and no-permanent-population parts are right, but the people there are not only scientists: stations are run by rotating crews that include engineers, medics, mechanics, cooks, pilots and logistics staff.
checks.fix: Under a 1959 treaty no nation may stake a new claim to it, and it has no permanent residents — only rotating crews of scientists and support staff.

checks.text: Home to emperor penguins and the South Pole, it is the southernmost continent.
checks.evidence: Southernmost continent, site of the South Pole, home to emperor penguins; treaty page covers the continent south of 60°S. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctic_Treaty_System

checks.fix: Its main step-pyramid, El Castillo, has about 91 steps per side, which with the top platform add up to 365, one per day of the year.

checks.fix: This animal is thought to 'hear' distant rumbles through the soles of its feet, picking up ground vibrations that may carry more than a mile.

checks.text: This shark's body runs warmer than the water around it, and it can launch itself clear of the surface to ambush a seal from below.

Off South Africa, its ambushes on Cape fur seals usually involve leaping or breaching out of the water, and white sharks typically ambush seals from below. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_white_shark

checks.text: The species of huge predatory fish behind the movie 'Jaws,' it is named for its pale underside.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: the common names refer to its white underside. Peter Benchley's novel Jaws and the film portray this species as a man-eater and set its public image. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_white_shark

checks.text: This country's national anthem comes from a poem 158 stanzas long, though usually only its first two stanzas are sung.
checks.evidence: The Hymn to Liberty has 158 stanzas, and its first two became Greece's national anthem in 1864. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hymn_to_Liberty

checks.text: Shipowners from this country control the world's largest merchant fleet by carrying capacity.
checks.evidence: 'As of 2020, Greece is the largest ship owner country in the world in terms of tonnage', about 364 million deadweight tons, though many ships use flags of convenience. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_Merchant_Marine

checks.text: Counting every islet, this country has up to 6,000 islands, yet fewer than 230 of them are inhabited.
checks.evidence: Estimates put Greece's islands at between 1,200 and 6,000; the Greek Tourism Organization counts 6,000 islands with 227 inhabited. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Greece

checks.text: With Athens as its capital and whitewashed Santorini for tourists, this is the home of the Parthenon.
checks.evidence: Athens is the capital and home of the Parthenon; Santorini is a major Greek tourist island. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Greece

checks.text: This 1984 film's makers tried using monkeys for its creatures, but dropped the idea when the test monkey panicked on being made to wear a creature's head.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: an earlier attempt to use monkeys was dropped because 'the test monkey panicked when made to wear a gremlin head.' Search results (Slashfilm, IMDb trivia) report Joe Dante confirming a rhesus monkey in a gremlin head bounced around the editing room before puppets were chosen. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gremlins

checks.text: In this film the heroine, Kate, explains that her father died climbing down the chimney dressed as Santa Claus, a speech studio executives wanted cut.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: Kate reveals her father died at Christmas dressed as Santa Claus, breaking his neck climbing down the chimney; studio executives 'insisted upon its removal', Dante refused. Mental Floss: Spielberg and some Warner Bros. executives wanted it removed. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gremlins https://www.mentalfloss.com/entertainment/movies/21-things-you-might-not-know-about-gremlins

checks.text: Criticism of the PG ratings given to this film and 'Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom' led Steven Spielberg to propose a new PG-13 rating, introduced that same year.
checks.evidence: Mental Floss: Temple of Doom and Gremlins were both rated PG and criticized; Spielberg proposed a rating between PG and R; Red Dawn was the first PG-13 release on August 10, 1984. Wikipedia: the MPAA created PG-13 'within two months of the film's release.' https://www.mentalfloss.com/entertainment/movies/21-things-you-might-not-know-about-gremlins https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gremlins

checks.text: This 1984 horror-comedy turns on three rules for caring for a cute furry creature: keep it out of the light, never let it get wet, and never feed it after midnight.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: keep the mogwai away from light, 'do not let it come in contact with water', and 'never let it eat after midnight.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gremlins

checks.text: This film's writer got its idea in 1990 while reading an Anne Rice vampire novel and wondering how a person would act if they could never die.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: idea came to Danny Rubin in 1990 while reading Anne Rice's The Vampire Lestat, musing on what one would do with limitless time. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groundhog_Day_(film)

checks.text: This film's star stopped speaking to its director after making it, and the pair, who had made Caddyshack and Ghostbusters together, barely talked for nearly two decades.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: after filming, Murray and Ramis 'did not speak to each other until shortly before Ramis's death in 2014' (about two decades). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groundhog_Day_(film)

checks.text: The animal co-star of this film bit its leading man on the knuckle through his gloves, then bit him again in the very same spot.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: the groundhog bit Murray on the knuckle; 'Although Murray was wearing gloves, the bite broke the skin'; later bit him again in the same spot. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groundhog_Day_(film)

checks.text: In this 1993 comedy, Bill Murray plays a grumpy TV weatherman who wakes up again and again on February 2 in Punxsutawney, Pennsylvania.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: 1993 comedy, Murray as Pittsburgh TV weatherman Phil Connors reliving February 2 in Punxsutawney. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groundhog_Day_(film)

checks.text: In 1974 an Iranian-born artist angry about the My Lai massacre case spray-painted 'KILL LIES ALL' across this painting in red, but it came off the varnish fairly easily.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: Shafrazi spray-painted 'KILL LIES ALL' in red on 28 Feb 1974, protesting Calley's habeas petition (My Lai); 'paint was removed with relative ease from the varnished surface'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guernica_(Picasso)

checks.text: A full-size tapestry copy of this painting hangs at the UN, and in 2003 it was covered with a blue curtain while Colin Powell made the case for war on Iraq.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: 'A full-size tapestry copy' hangs at UN HQ; in 2003 'a large blue curtain was placed to cover' it during Colin Powell's press appearances. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guernica_(Picasso)

checks.text: Its artist refused to let this painting go to Spain until democratic freedoms returned there, so it stayed at New York's Museum of Modern Art until 1981.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: Picasso said it should not go to Spain until liberty and democracy were established; 'Until 1981, Guernica itself remained at MoMA'. It toured widely 1939-1956 while in MoMA's custody, but the clue matches the source. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guernica_(Picasso)

checks.text: Picasso painted this huge black-and-white canvas in 1937 after German and Italian planes bombed a Basque town during the Spanish Civil War.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: 1937 painting responding to the German/Italian bombing of the Basque town of Guernica. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guernica_(Picasso)

checks.text: A 1930s cast-aluminum model of this instrument, nicknamed the 'Frying Pan', was played lying flat across the player's lap.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia says the Frying Pan, developed in 1931-32, was made of cast aluminum and was the first electric lap steel; a lap steel is played flat across the lap. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frying_Pan_(guitar)

checks.text: Andrés Segovia, who gave his first public concert in Granada at 16 in 1909, spent decades winning this instrument a place in the concert hall.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia says his first public performance was in Granada in 1909, when he was 16 (born 21 February 1893). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andr%C3%A9s_Segovia

checks.text: In 2020 one of these instruments, played on a famous 1993 'MTV Unplugged' set, sold at auction for just over $6 million, then a record.
checks.evidence: CBS News, June 2020: Cobain's guitar from MTV Unplugged (taped 18 November 1993) sold for a record $6 million at Julien's Auctions. https://www.cbsnews.com/amp/news/kurt-cobains-mtv-unplugged-guitar-sells-for-record-6-million-at-auction

checks.text: This six-stringed instrument, played by flamenco masters and rock stars alike, is among the world's most popular.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia says it typically has six strings, is used in flamenco and is widely used in rock music. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar

checks.text: This painter's three ceiling paintings for the University of Vienna were called pornographic by critics, and all three burned when German forces set fire to an Austrian castle in May 1945.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: Philosophy, Medicine and Jurisprudence called 'pornographic'; all three destroyed in May 1945 when retreating German forces burned Schloss Immendorf. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustav_Klimt

checks.text: For a 1902 exhibition honoring Beethoven, this painter made a wall frieze in which the composer's face resembled that of the Vienna opera director Mahler.
checks.evidence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beethoven_Frieze https://www.mahlerfoundation.org/?p=8445 (knight 'said to be' a portrait of Mahler)
checks.problem: The Beethoven Frieze has no portrait of Beethoven; it illustrates Wagner's reading of the Ninth Symphony. The figure said to resemble Mahler is the golden-armored knight ('the Well-Armed Strong One'). The Klimt Wikipedia line about 'the face on the Beethoven portrait' is garbled, and the Beethoven Frieze article does not support it.
checks.fix: For a 1902 exhibition honoring Beethoven, this painter made a wall frieze whose knight in golden armor is said to bear the features of Vienna opera director Mahler.

checks.text: This painter's portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer sold for a reported $135 million in 2006, and an heir's long legal fight to recover it became the film 'Woman in Gold'.
checks.evidence: Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I sold for a reported $135 million in 2006; Maria Altmann's case is the basis of 'Woman in Gold'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portrait_of_Adele_Bloch-Bauer_I

checks.text: This Austrian painter, a founder of the Vienna Secession, added real gold leaf to 'The Kiss', his painting of a couple locked in an embrace.
checks.evidence: Founding member and president of the Vienna Secession (1897); The Kiss is oil and gold leaf on canvas. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Kiss_(Klimt)

checks.text: This Greek god's mistress, a river nymph named Minthe, was trampled by his jealous wife in one version of her myth and turned into garden mint.
checks.evidence: Strabo 8.3.14: Minthe 'was trampled under foot by Kore' and changed into garden-mint (hedyosmos); Oppian has Demeter do it, so 'in one version' is right. https://www.theoi.com/Nymphe/NympheMinthe.html

checks.text: Worshippers sacrificed black animals such as sheep to this god, and the person making the offering had to turn his face away.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia Hades: black animals such as sheep were sacrificed to him and the person offering averted his face. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hades

checks.text: During the war against the Titans, the Cyclopes forged this god a helmet of invisibility, while his brothers got a thunderbolt and a trident.
checks.evidence: Apollodorus 1.2.1: during the Titan war the Cyclopes gave Zeus thunder and lightning, Pluto a helmet, Poseidon a trident. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclopes

checks.text: This Greek god ruled the underworld, abducted Persephone to be his queen, and had the three-headed dog Cerberus guarding his gates.
checks.evidence: Standard myth. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hades

checks.text: Kericho, a tea-growing town in Kenya's highlands, is reputed to hold the world record for the most days of this weather in a single year.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia's Kericho article says it is 'reputed to hold the record for the highest number of hail occurrences in a year' and describes it as a highland tea town; the Hail article says 'Kericho reached the world record for 132 days of hail in one year.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hail

checks.text: In the Middle Ages, Europeans rang church bells and fired cannons to ward this off, and some farmers still fire acetylene 'cannons' at storms, with no evidence they work.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia's Hail article says people in Europe used to ring church bells and fire cannons to try to prevent hail, and that modern hail cannons are updated versions; the Hail cannon article says they ignite acetylene and oxygen and that there is 'no scientific evidence' they work. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hail_cannon

checks.text: In 2010 a piece of this that fell in Vivian, South Dakota, set US records at 8 inches across and almost 2 pounds.
checks.evidence: NWS Aberdeen: the 23 July 2010 Vivian, SD stone measured 8.0 inches in diameter and weighed 1.9375 lb, breaking the US records for diameter and weight (not circumference). https://www.weather.gov/abr/vivianhailstone

checks.text: These lumps of ice form in thunderstorm updrafts, and weather spotters describe their size by comparing them to peas, golf balls and softballs.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: the storm's updraft blows forming hailstones up the cloud; the NWS size chart uses a pea, a golf ball and a softball as references. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hail

checks.text: This object appears in the Bayeux Tapestry, where its 1066 visit was taken as an omen before the Norman conquest of England.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: the comet was seen in England in 1066 and taken as an omen; Harold II died at Hastings that year; the Bayeux Tapestry shows the comet. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halley%27s_Comet

checks.text: Mark Twain was born in 1835, the year of one of this comet's visits, and died in 1910 during its next, as he had said he expected to.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: Twain was born 30 November 1835, two weeks after perihelion, and died 21 April 1910, the day after the 1910 perihelion; he had said 'I expect to go out with it.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halley%27s_Comet

checks.text: An English astronomer realized that several past sightings were one returning object and foretold its comeback, which arrived after his death.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: Halley linked the comets of 1531, 1607 and 1682 as one object and predicted its return for 1758; he died in 1742, and it was seen again on 25 December 1758. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halley%27s_Comet

checks.text: This most famous of comets last swept past Earth in 1986 and is due back in 2061, on a cycle of about 75 or 76 years.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: last perihelion 8 February 1986, next 28 July 2061, period listed as 74.7 years (it varies, typically 75-76). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halley%27s_Comet

checks.text: A female of this fish at a Nebraska zoo gave birth in 2001 without ever mating with a male.
checks.evidence: A bonnethead (a small hammerhead species) at Omaha's Henry Doorly Zoo gave birth in December 2001 with no male; DNA tests in 2007 confirmed parthenogenesis. https://www.sciencenews.org/article/virgin-birth-shark-has-daughter-without-dad

checks.text: One species of this fish spends up to 90% of its time swimming tilted on its side, using its tall dorsal fin like a wing to save energy.

checks.text: Named for the tool its wide, flattened skull resembles, this predatory fish sweeps it side to side to find stingrays buried in sand.
checks.evidence: Great hammerheads swing their heads in broad arcs over the sea floor to pick up the electrical signals of stingrays buried in sand, using the head like a metal detector's sensor plate. https://mail.elasmo-research.org/education/ecology/sandy-gt_hammerhead.htm

checks.text: This 2012 track's opening 'Con los terroristas!' was sampled without permission from reggaeton star Héctor Delgado, who had quit music in 2008 for evangelical Christianity.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: Héctor Luis Delgado announced his retirement from music on September 3, 2008 after becoming a born-again Christian, joining an evangelical church; his 'con los terroristas' line was used without credit in the opening of Baauer's track https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%A9ctor_el_Father ; the sample was not cleared, and the track was released in 2012 https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlem_Shake_(song)

checks.text: This track debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 in the very week the chart began counting YouTube views, only the 21st song ever to start at the top.

checks.text: In 2013 up to 15 Australian miners were fired, and the FAA looked into a Frontier Airlines flight, after people filmed themselves doing this craze.

checks.evidence: Harry wears glasses, is a wizard created by Rowling, and the seven-book series centres on his struggle against Voldemort. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Potter_(character)

checks.text: This tropical Pacific state, birthplace of surfing and the greeting 'aloha,' was the 50th to join the U.S.

checks.problem: Surfing began with the ancient Polynesians generally, not in this state alone; calling it the 'birthplace of surfing' overstates it. 'Aloha' and 50th state are fine.
checks.fix: This tropical Pacific state, where ancient chiefs rode the surf and 'aloha' is the greeting, was the 50th to join the U.S.

checks.text: This organ is almost never where cancer starts, partly because its muscle cells rarely divide.

checks.text: In 1929 a 24-year-old German doctor threaded a catheter from a vein in his own arm into this organ and took an X-ray to prove it.

checks.problem: The age of 24 is not supported. Forssmann was born on 29 August 1904, and sources (NPR and others) describe him as 25 when he did the experiment. Wikipedia gives no month, so he was 24 or 25 depending on the date.

checks.fix: This creature was the emblem on the sleeve badge of Britain's wartime airborne troops, and a Normandy canal bridge they seized by glider in June 1944 was renamed after it weeks later.

checks.problem: The heart (Tombaugh Regio) is not one glacier. Only its western lobe, Sputnik Planitia, is a nitrogen-ice glacier basin; the eastern lobe is uplands coated in nitrogen frost.
checks.fix: A 2015 flyby beamed back photos of a vast heart-shaped bright patch, its western lobe a glacier of frozen nitrogen.

checks.evidence: Wikipedia: name commonly glossed 'feathered serpent' (more precisely 'quetzal-feathered serpent'); Quetzalcoatlus named after him in 1975. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quetzalcoatl

checks.text: This hazard appears in the Bayeux Tapestry, which shows the future King Harold pulling two Norman soldiers out of it at the river Couesnon near Mont-Saint-Michel.
checks.evidence: Crossing the Couesnon past Mont-Saint-Michel, 'two soldiers are saved by Harold' from quicksand; caption 'Duke Harold pulled them from quicksand'. https://sajou.fr/en/blog/the-bayeux-tapestry-part-two-n54

checks.text: A 2005 study in Nature worked out that pulling a trapped foot out of this at one centimeter per second takes about as much force as lifting a car.
checks.evidence: 2005 Nature study (Khaldoun et al.): removing a foot at 1 cm/s takes the force needed to lift a car. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quicksand ; https://www.nature.com/news/2005/050926/full/news050926-9.html

checks.text: This has a density of about 2 grams per cubic centimeter, so a person floats in it, and a piece of aluminum rests on top until movement liquefies it.
checks.evidence: Density about 2 g/cm3, so a human floats; aluminium floats on top until motion liquefies the sand. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quicksand

checks.text: This soupy, waterlogged sand was a favorite movie peril in the 1960s, when almost 3% of all films showed someone sinking into clay, mud or sand.
checks.evidence: Peaked in the 1960s, 'when almost 3% of all films showed characters sinking in clay, mud, or sand' (2010 Slate, cited). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quicksand

checks.text: This animal became a pet craze in Japan after a 1977 cartoon, with up to 1,500 of them imported each year.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia says the anime aired in 1977 and that afterward up to 1,500 raccoons were imported into Japan as pets each year; Nautilus and Fox News/Smithsonian give the same yearly figure (Atlas Obscura's 'a month' is an outlier). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rascal_the_Raccoon

checks.text: This animal's German name, Waschbär, means 'washing bear,' because it seems to wash its food in water.
checks.evidence: Waschbär is the German word for raccoon, a compound of waschen ('to wash') read as 'wash-bear', because raccoons appear to wash their food. https://languagehat.com/how-to-name-animals-in-german/

checks.text: In 2016, Toronto spent about $31 million on new green bins designed to keep this animal out.
checks.evidence: Toronto began rolling out raccoon-resistant green bins in April 2016 under a 10-year Rehrig Pacific contract estimated at just over $31 million; NPR reported the city spent CA$31 million on them in 2016. https://globalnews.ca/news/2667460/city-of-toronto-rolls-out-raccoon-proof-green-bins

checks.text: Nicknamed the 'trash panda,' this masked bandit is a familiar backyard visitor.
checks.evidence: 'Trash panda' is a well-known nickname, and the masked face is common knowledge; the same coverage describes Toronto's 'uber raccoon' raiding garbage. https://www.npr.org/2018/09/16/647599627/theres-no-stopping-toronto-s-uber-raccoon

checks.text: This optical sight is different for every viewer: no two people see exactly the same one, since it depends on where the light meets each person's eyes.
checks.evidence: Mental Floss: it is 'scientifically impossible for two people to see exactly the same thing', because each observer's line from the sun through the bow's center passes through their own eyes. (The cited USGS page does not say this.) https://www.mentalfloss.com/article/652449/why-no-two-people-see-same-rainbow

checks.text: It is really a full circle of light, but from the ground you only ever see the top arc.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: 'In theory, every rainbow is a circle, but from the ground, usually only its upper half can be seen'; Science Focus says the ground hides the lower part and planes can see the full ring. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow
checks.problem: 'Only ever' is too strong. Wikipedia says from the ground 'usually only its upper half can be seen'; from a high vantage point, or with spray close by, more of the circle is visible.
checks.fix: It is really a full circle of light, but from the ground the horizon usually hides all but the top arc.

checks.text: Sometimes a fainter second one appears just outside it, with its colors in reverse order.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: a second arc about 10 degrees outside the primary, always fainter, with colors in reverse order. (The cited AMS glossary returned 403.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow

checks.text: This arc of red-through-violet colors stretches across the sky when the sun shines during or after rain.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia and Science Focus describe a colored arc formed when sunlight from behind the viewer is refracted and reflected in raindrops. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow

checks.text: This band of light always sits about 42 degrees from the point directly opposite the sun, an angle René Descartes calculated in 1637 with a water-filled glass sphere.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia's Rainbow article says the bow is centred on the antisolar point (the observer's head shadow) and that "The base of the cone forms a circle at an angle of 40-42 degrees to the line between the observer's head and their shadow", so "about 42 degrees" matches the primary bow's outer edge; the same article says that in his 1637 treatise Discourse on Method Descartes "experimented with passing rays of light through a large glass sphere filled with water" to work out the rainbow's angles. Histories of the calculation agree he put the maximum radius at about 41 degrees 47 minutes, i.e. about 42 degrees. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow

checks.text: Isaac Newton first counted only five colors in this display, then added orange and indigo so the total would match the seven notes of a musical scale.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia's Rainbow article says Newton "originally (1672) divided the spectrum into five main colours" and later "includ[ed] orange and indigo, giving seven main colours by analogy to the number of notes in a musical scale"; the ROYGBIV article says the same ("Originally he used only five colors", then added orange and indigo "to match the number of musical notes in the major scale"). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow

checks.text: Released by colonists in the 1800s for sport hunting, this predator now threatens native wildlife across Australia.
checks.evidence: Victorian government material says foxes were introduced for recreational hunting in 1855, were established in the wild by the early 1870s and spread across most of Australia; predation by foxes is a listed key threatening process for native fauna. https://agriculture.vic.gov.au/biosecurity/pest-animals/established-pest-animal-species/red-fox

checks.text: When this predator pounces on mice hidden under snow, it most often leaps toward the north-east, which suggests it may aim using Earth's magnetic field.
checks.evidence: Červený's study of about 600 mousing jumps by 84 foxes found a strong preference for jumping north-east (about 20 degrees off magnetic north), with higher success; the authors suggest a magnetic targeting system. https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/foxes-use-the-earths-magnetic-field-as-a-targeting-system

checks.text: The most widespread wild member of the dog family, it gives a piercing scream in the winter mating season that people often mistake for someone in distress.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia calls the red fox the most widely distributed member of the order Carnivora, so it is also the most widespread wild canid; TheJournal.ie says its mating calls can be mistaken for a person's scream, in the December-February mating season. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_fox and https://www.thejournal.ie/?p=5660806&utm_source=shortlink

checks.text: Rusty-orange with black 'socks,' this cunning hunter is the one a pack of hounds famously chases.
checks.evidence: The red fox is the quarry of traditional fox hunting with hounds and is described as preying on small animals; its reddish coat with dark legs is standard. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_fox

checks.text: This tissue has the greatest continuous energy demand of any part of the human body, greater even than the brain's.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: 'the part of the body with the greatest continuous energy demand'; 'even greater than that of the brain'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retina

checks.text: The tiny bright dots that dart about when you stare at a clear blue sky are white blood cells in vessels lying in front of this tissue.
checks.evidence: Blue field entoptic phenomenon: dots seen looking into bright blue light such as the sky are white blood cells in capillaries in front of the retina. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_field_entoptic_phenomenon

checks.text: This tissue grows out of the embryonic brain, and it is the only part of the nervous system that can be seen without an invasive procedure.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: retina originates as an outgrowth of the embryonic diencephalon; 'the only part of the nervous system that can be visualized noninvasively'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retina

checks.text: This thin layer at the back of the eye holds the rods and cones, and its name comes from the Latin word for 'net'.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: from Latin rete, 'net'; holds rods and cones. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retina

checks.text: A group of these animals is called a 'crash,' and they use shared dung heaps called middens to leave scent messages for each other.
checks.evidence: A group is sometimes called a 'crash' https://sandiegozoowildlifealliance.org/story-hub/2015/05/08/24-rhino-facts-you-should-know/ ; white rhinos use dung middens to signal sex, age, territory and oestrous state https://newatlas.com/rhinos-poo-information-centers/47340 (search result)

checks.text: Badly near-sighted, this huge, thick-skinned grazer leans on sharp hearing and smell to sense trouble.
checks.evidence: White rhinos are grazers, black rhinos browsers https://rhinos.org/blog/oppositeday-grazers-versus-browsers/ ; black rhino eyesight comparatively good per studies https://www.sanparks.org/conservation/parks/marakele-national-park/primary-consumers-herbivores/black-rhino (search results)
checks.problem: 'Grazer' fits only white (and partly Indian) rhinos; black, Javan and Sumatran rhinos are browsers. 'Badly near-sighted' is the common belief, but studies suggest black rhino eyesight is better than assumed.
checks.fix: With weak eyesight, this huge, thick-skinned plant-eater leans on sharp hearing and smell to sense trouble.

checks.text: Its horn, the reason poachers hunt it, has no bone in it at all; it is keratin, the same stuff as your fingernails.
checks.evidence: San Diego Zoo: rhino horn is made of keratin, the same material as fingernails (no bone core). https://sandiegozoowildlifealliance.org/story-hub/2015/05/08/24-rhino-facts-you-should-know/

checks.text: This massive horned herbivore, second only to the elephant in land-animal size, wallows in mud to keep cool.
checks.evidence: San Diego Zoo: 'White rhinos are the largest rhino species and the second largest land mammal'; photo of a rhino in a mudbath. https://sandiegozoowildlifealliance.org/story-hub/2015/05/08/24-rhino-facts-you-should-know/
checks.problem: Only the white rhino is the second-largest land mammal; Sumatran and other species are far smaller, so the claim is overstated for rhinos in general.
checks.fix: This massive horned herbivore, whose biggest species is second only to the elephant among land animals, wallows in mud to keep cool.

checks.text: Albrecht Dürer's famous 1515 woodcut of this animal was based on a written description and a brief sketch; he never saw the animal itself.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: Dürer never saw the rhinoceros. He based the 1515 woodcut on an anonymous written description and a brief sketch of an Indian rhinoceros that had arrived in Lisbon. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%BCrer%27s_Rhinoceros

checks.text: Oxpeckers riding on this weak-sighted animal give alarm calls when people approach; in a 2020 study it spotted walkers every time the birds were aboard, but only 23 percent of the time without them.
checks.evidence: Victoria University (April 10, 2020), on a 2020 Current Biology study: black rhinos have poor vision, and oxpeckers give alarm calls when humans approach. Rhinos carrying oxpeckers detected approaching humans 100% of the time, and rhinos without them only 23% of the time. https://www.vu.edu.au/about-vu/news-events/news/black-rhinos-eavesdrop-on-alarm-calls-of-hitchhiking-oxpeckers-to-avoid-humans

checks.text: This city became the only European capital outside Europe when Portugal's royal court, fleeing Napoleon's invasion, moved there in 1808.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: when the Portuguese Royal Court moved to Brazil in 1808 the city 'became the only European capital outside of Europe'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro

checks.text: Its Maracanã stadium drew an official crowd of 173,850 for the deciding match of the 1950 World Cup, still a record for a World Cup game.
checks.evidence: Official attendance 173,850 at the decisive match of the 1950 final round, an all-time high for paid spectators; it remains the largest World Cup crowd. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uruguay_v_Brazil_(1950_FIFA_World_Cup)

checks.text: Europeans first reached its bay on New Year's Day 1502, and its name recalls the month of their arrival.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: 'Europeans first encountered Guanabara Bay on 1 January 1502 (hence Rio de Janeiro, January River)'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro

checks.text: This Brazilian city, famed for Copacabana beach and Carnival, hosted the 2016 Summer Olympics.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: host of the 2016 Summer Olympics; known for Copacabana beach and carnival. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro

checks.text: After a New York taxi hit this writer's baby son, he helped invent a brain-drain valve for children with hydrocephalus, and its co-inventors agreed never to profit from it.
checks.evidence: Wade-Dahl-Till valve article: Theo got hydrocephalus after a taxi hit him in 1960; 'The co-inventors agreed never to accept any profit from the invention.' The accident was in New York, when Theo was a baby. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wade-Dahl-Till_valve

checks.text: This writer wrote the screenplays for the James Bond film You Only Live Twice and for Chitty Chitty Bang Bang, both adapted from Ian Fleming novels.
checks.evidence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chitty_Chitty_Bang_Bang (screenplay by Roald Dahl and Ken Hughes)
checks.problem: Dahl wrote You Only Live Twice, but he co-wrote Chitty Chitty Bang Bang with the director Ken Hughes (Richard Maibaum added dialogue). 'Wrote the screenplays' overstates his part in Chitty.
checks.fix: This writer wrote the screenplay for the James Bond film You Only Live Twice and co-wrote the one for Chitty Chitty Bang Bang, both adapted from Ian Fleming novels.

checks.text: As a schoolboy at Repton, this writer helped taste-test new chocolates that the Cadbury company sent to the school.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: 'the Cadbury chocolate company occasionally sent boxes of new chocolates to the school to be tested by pupils.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roald_Dahl

checks.text: This British author wrote Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, Matilda, The BFG and James and the Giant Peach.
checks.evidence: Standard bibliography. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roald_Dahl

checks.text: The first edition of this 1719 novel named its hero as the author, so many readers took the book for a true travel account.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: 'The first edition credited the work's protagonist Robinson Crusoe as its author', leading many readers to take it as a true travelogue. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robinson_Crusoe

checks.text: In his treatise 'Emile', Rousseau made this the one book his young pupil is allowed to read before the age of twelve.
checks.evidence: https://newlearningonline.com/new-learning/chapter-2/supporting-material-1/jean-jacques-rousseau-on-emiles-education ; https://www.gutenberg.org/etext/5427 (Emile, Books II-III)
checks.problem: Wikipedia says 'before the age of twelve', but Rousseau's own text says the reverse: in Book II he writes that Emile 'at twelve years old, will hardly know what a book is', and Crusoe comes up in Book III (the ages 12-15 stage) as 'the first book Emile will read', which 'for a long time' will be his whole library. So it is the first and only book, not a book read before twelve.
checks.fix: In his treatise 'Emile', Rousseau made this the first book his young pupil is allowed to read, and for a long time his entire library.

checks.text: In 1966 Chile renamed the Pacific island where castaway Alexander Selkirk spent over four years after this novel's hero, to attract tourists.
checks.evidence: Selkirk was marooned 'four years and four months'; on 1 Jan 1966 President Frei renamed Mas a Tierra 'after Defoe's fictional character to attract tourists'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Selkirk

checks.text: This Daniel Defoe novel follows a shipwrecked sailor who spends 28 years on an island and names his companion Friday.
checks.evidence: Crusoe 'spends 28 years on a remote tropical desert island'; names his companion Friday. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robinson_Crusoe

checks.text: This game's first known mention is in a Chinese book from around 1600, which calls it 'shoushiling' and claims Han dynasty warlords played it.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: 'The first known mention of the game was in the book Wuzazu by the Ming-dynasty writer Xie Zhaozhe (fl. c. 1600), who wrote that the game dated back to the time of the Han dynasty, where it was played by warlords. In the book, the game was called shoushiling.' The clue correctly frames the Han claim as the book's claim. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_paper_scissors

checks.text: In 2005 Christie's beat Sotheby's at this game, on an 11-year-old's advice, to win the right to sell a Japanese firm's art collection worth about $20 million.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: in 2005 Maspro Denkoh's CEO had Christie's and Sotheby's play; Christie's chose scissors on the advice of a director's 11-year-old twin daughters and won; the collection sold for $20 million. Mental Floss: advice came from 'a colleague's 11-year-old twins, Flora and Alice'. Minor note: the advice came from twins, but one of them gave the reasoning, so the singular holds. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_paper_scissors https://www.mentalfloss.com/article/64401/time-sothebys-and-christies-played-rock-paper-scissors-cezanne

checks.text: Male side-blotched lizards come in three throat colors, and biologists compare the way their rival mating tactics balance out to this game.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: the common side-blotched lizard has three male throat-color morphs; 'orange beats blue, blue beats yellow, and yellow beats orange' in competing for females, mirroring the game. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_paper_scissors

checks.text: In this hand game, a closed fist beats two fingers held in a V, the V beats a flat hand, and the flat hand covers the fist.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: rock is a closed fist, paper a flat hand, scissors two fingers in a V; rock beats scissors, scissors beats paper, 'paper covers rock'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_paper_scissors

checks.text: At this empire's height, a traveller could go from Britain to the Persian Gulf without ever leaving its borders.
checks.evidence: Under Trajan, 'it was quite possible for a Roman to travel from Britain to the Persian Gulf without leaving Roman territory' (lands east of the Euphrates held only 116-117). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Roman_Empire

checks.text: One of this empire's rulers was said to have planned to make his favourite horse, Incitatus, a consul.
checks.evidence: Suetonius and Dio report Caligula planned to make Incitatus consul; the article treats it as an unconfirmed story, which the clue's 'was said to' reflects. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incitatus

checks.text: In 8 BC a summer month was renamed to honour this empire's first emperor, who chose it because several of his great victories fell in it.
checks.evidence: 'In 8 BC, the month was renamed in honor of Emperor Augustus'; he chose it because it was the time of several of his great triumphs, including the conquest of Egypt. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/August

checks.text: Spanning the Mediterranean it called 'our sea,' this ancient superpower spread Latin and its legions across Europe.
checks.evidence: Mare Nostrum, Latin for 'Our Sea', was the Roman term for the Mediterranean once Roman control reached from Iberia to Egypt. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mare_Nostrum

checks.text: For centuries, people in this city have stuck anonymous satirical verses on a battered ancient statue called Pasquino, which gave English the word 'pasquinade.'
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: anonymous satirical verses have been attached to the 'battered' Hellenistic-style statue since the early 16th century, giving English the word 'pasquinade.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasquino

checks.text: This city's visitors toss about 3,000 euros a day into one of its fountains, and the money goes to a charity that feeds people in need.
checks.evidence: Euronews: about 3,000 euros lands in the Trevi Fountain each day, and since 2001 it goes to the charity Caritas, funding soup kitchens and shelters. https://euronews.com/travel/2024/03/29/tourists-throw-over-1-million-into-italys-trevi-fountain-each-year-heres-what-happens-to-i

checks.text: A domed temple in this city, built about 1,900 years ago, still has the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: the Pantheon was completed around AD 126 and its dome 'is still the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantheon,_Rome

checks.text: Nicknamed the 'Eternal City,' this Italian capital straddles the Tiber River.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: known as the 'Eternal City', capital of Italy, lying along the Tiber. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome

checks.text: What is usually called the earliest version of this story, published in 1476, is set in Siena and ends with the hero beheaded and the heroine dying of grief.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: Masuccio's 1476 tale is the 'earliest known version', set in Siena; 'Mariotto is caught and beheaded and Ganozza dies of grief'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romeo_and_Juliet

checks.text: This play squeezes into four to six days a romance that lasts nine months in the 1562 English poem it was based on.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: the play 'spans a period of four to six days, in contrast to Brooke's poems spanning nine months'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romeo_and_Juliet

checks.text: In this play a friar's potion is meant to make someone seem dead for exactly 'two and forty hours.'
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: Friar Laurence's potion gives a deathlike state for 'two and forty hours' (Act 4 Sc 1). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romeo_and_Juliet

checks.text: The word 'balcony' never appears in this Shakespeare tragedy about the 'star-cross'd' teenage lovers of Verona, despite its famous balcony scene.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: 'the original Shakespeare play does not contain a balcony'; Juliet appears at a window. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romeo_and_Juliet

checks.text: One of this legendary pair is said to have vanished in a sudden thunderstorm while reviewing his army, and was later worshipped as the god Quirinus.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: Romulus 'disappeared in a whirlwind during a sudden and violent storm, as he was reviewing his troops on the Campus Martius'; his cult 'later became assimilated with the cult of Quirinus'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romulus

checks.text: To settle which of them would name and rule a new city, this pair watched the sky from two hills; one saw six vultures first, but the other then saw twelve.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: 'Remus sighted six vultures over the Aventine Hill, then Romulus saw a flight of twelve above the Palatine Hill'; Remus claimed priority for seeing first, Romulus for seeing more. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romulus

checks.text: Figures of this pair were added to a famous bronze in Rome's Capitoline Museums in the late 15th century, and radiocarbon tests suggest the animal above them is medieval.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: twins 'added in the late 15th century AD, probably by sculptor Antonio del Pollaiuolo'; radiocarbon dating of casting-core residues indicates the wolf was made between 1021 and 1153 AD (dating contested by some scholars); housed in the Capitoline Museums. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitoline_Wolf

checks.text: Set adrift on the Tiber as babies, these twin sons of Mars were suckled by a she-wolf; one later killed the other and founded Rome.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: the twin sons of Mars were set adrift on the Tiber, suckled by a she-wolf, and after the augury dispute Romulus killed Remus and founded Rome. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romulus

checks.text: This gadget's prototype was called DustPuppy, because like a puppy it would try very hard to please but might sometimes mess up.
checks.evidence: Joe Jones in Nautilus: DustPuppy was chosen to set expectations; like a puppy it 'would try very hard to please' but 'might sometimes mess up'. https://nautil.us/dont-fear-the-robot-237802/

checks.text: Amazon agreed in 2022 to buy this gadget's maker for about $1.7 billion, but the deal collapsed in January 2024 over EU competition concerns.
checks.evidence: The August 2022 agreement was $61 a share, about $1.7 billion; the price was cut in 2023 (hence Bloomberg's $1.4 billion), and the companies ended the deal on 29 January 2024 saying it had 'no path to regulatory approval' in the EU. The clue's 'agreed in 2022 ... about $1.7 billion' is accurate. https://sharecast.com/amp/news/international-companies/amazon-irobot-abandon-merger-due-to-eu-opposition--15985368.html https://www.cepro.com/news/amazon-irobot-terminate-acquisition-deal-due-to-eu-regulatory-hurdles/133138/

checks.text: In 2016 this machine's maker admitted 'we see this a lot' after viral reports of the machines smearing dog poop across owners' floors.
checks.evidence: Guardian (August 2016), cited by Wikipedia: 'Roomba creator responds to reports of poopocalypse: We see this a lot'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roomba

checks.text: This disc-shaped robot vacuum, launched by iRobot in 2002, is held by the Smithsonian as 'the first successful domestic robot.'
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: introduced September 2002; the National Museum of American History holds an original, noted as 'the first successful domestic robot'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roomba

checks.text: This flowering shrub has grown against the apse of Germany's Hildesheim Cathedral for about 700 years, and its roots survived the 1945 bombing that wrecked the church.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: grows against the eastern apse of Hildesheim Cathedral; documentation verifies about 700 years; 1945 bombing destroyed above-ground parts but the roots survived. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thousand-year_Rose

checks.text: Apples, pears, cherries, almonds and strawberries all belong to the plant family named after this flower.
checks.evidence: Rosaceae includes apples, pears, cherries, almonds (Prunus) and strawberries (Fragaria); family named for Rosa. https://www.britannica.com/plant/Rosaceae

checks.text: In 1986 Ronald Reagan proclaimed this flower the national floral emblem of the United States, noting that George Washington had bred them.
checks.evidence: Reagan Proclamation 5574, 20 Nov 1986: 'Our first President, George Washington, bred roses'. https://www.reaganlibrary.gov/research/speeches/112086a

checks.text: In Romeo and Juliet, Juliet says that this flower would smell as sweet by any other name.
checks.evidence: Juliet, Act 2 Scene 2: that which we call a rose by any other name would smell as sweet. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_rose_by_any_other_name_would_smell_as_sweet

checks.text: This character's creator, a Montgomery Ward copywriter, first tried the names Rollo and Reginald, according to his draft manuscripts now held at Dartmouth College.
checks.evidence: Farmers' Almanac: 'Draft manuscripts held at Dartmouth College, May's alma mater, show Rollo and Reginald came first'; Robert L. May wrote the story for Montgomery Ward. https://www.farmersalmanac.com/the-real-story-behind-rudolph

checks.text: A 6-inch puppet of this character from a 1960s TV special sold with its Santa puppet for $368,000 in 2020, years after Antiques Roadshow valued the pair at $8,000 to $10,000.

checks.text: Gene Autry first turned down the song about this character, written by its creator's brother-in-law, but his wife talked him into it, and his 1949 recording hit No. 1.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: Autry 'first rejected it, but his wife convinced him'; recorded 1949, it 'hit No. 1 in the US charts during Christmas 1949'; Johnny Marks was May's brother-in-law. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolph,_the_Red-Nosed_Reindeer_(song)

checks.text: In a 1964 Rankin/Bass stop-motion TV special, this young outcast visits the Island of Misfit Toys and later lights the way for Santa's sleigh through a snowstorm.
