checks.text: This body system's hyoid, a horseshoe-shaped piece in the neck, is the only one of its parts not joined to any other.
checks.evidence: The hyoid is a 'horseshoe-shaped bone' in the neck and 'the only bone in the human body that is not connected to any other bones.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyoid_bone

checks.text: In adults this body system is constantly rebuilt, with roughly a tenth of it replaced every year.
checks.evidence: Adult bone remodeling runs at 'about 10% per year.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bone_remodeling

checks.text: A rattling one is a Halloween staple, and it is what an X-ray reveals beneath the skin.
checks.evidence: Common knowledge: X-rays show the bones, and skeletons are a Halloween staple. The skeleton article (opened) covers the bony framework. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skeleton

checks.text: This body system doubles as a gland: in mice it releases a hormone reported to tell the pancreas to put out more insulin and to sharpen memory, though later mouse studies could not repeat the insulin result.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia on osteocalcin: the uncarboxylated form acts as a hormone made in bone and causes pancreatic beta cells to release more insulin, and it plays a role in spatial learning and memory. Columbia University's report on Oury et al. (Cell, 2013) confirms the memory work was in mice: mice lacking osteocalcin had smaller hippocampi and impaired learning and memory. The 2020 PLOS Genetics commentary "Lack of reproducibility in osteocalcin-deficient mice" records that Moriishi and Komori, and Diegel et al., found glucose metabolism normal in osteocalcin-null mice, including insulin tolerance testing, so the metabolic result did not replicate. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7319276/

checks.text: This body system is a Halloween staple, rattling on doorsteps every October, and it is what an X-ray reveals beneath the skin.
checks.evidence: MedlinePlus: X-rays "send a small amount of radiation through your body to create pictures of bones and organs," with bone blocking the most radiation and appearing white, so the image shows bone beneath the skin. Wikipedia's Halloween article lists skeletons first among the "traditionally macabre symbols" used to decorate yards, public spaces and houses. https://medlineplus.gov/xrays.html

checks.text: This toy's inventor left his wife, six children and a nearly bankrupt company in 1960 to join an evangelical group in Bolivia, and she rebuilt the business.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia Richard T. James: in 1960 went to Bolivia to join Wycliffe Bible Translators, leaving 'his wife, six children, and nearly-bankrupt company'; Betty ran the business. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_T._James

checks.text: During the Vietnam War, soldiers used this toy as a portable antenna for their radios.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia Slinky: 'During the Vietnam War, it was used as a portable antenna for local HF communication.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slinky

checks.text: This toy sat unsold at a Philadelphia department store in 1945 until its inventor demonstrated it on a ramp, and then the first 400 sold out in about 90 minutes.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia Richard T. James: 'Originally displayed in a static position, none of the toys sold' until he demonstrated it on a ramp; first run of 400 sold out within 90 minutes. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_T._James

checks.text: This coiled metal spring toy is famous for walking down a flight of stairs end over end.
checks.evidence: Well established. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slinky

checks.text: A green alga not known to grow anywhere else lives in this mammal's fur, tinting its coat a mossy green.
checks.evidence: The host-specific green alga Trichophilus in sloth hair 'has not been found to occur in any other environment'. http://blogs.biomedcentral.com/on-biology/2010/04/14/sloth-fur-has-symbiotic-relationship-with-green-algae/

checks.text: Its digestion is so slow that a single leafy meal can take weeks to break down.
checks.evidence: 'The digestive process can take a month or more to complete.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sloth

checks.text: It climbs down from the treetops only about once a week — to relieve itself — and can hold its breath longer than a dolphin.
checks.evidence: Sloths descend about once every eight days (three-toed about once a week) and can slow their heart to hold their breath up to 40 minutes, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sloth ; the sloth-vs-dolphin comparison is given without cited studies. https://www.thenakedscientists.com/node/191657
checks.problem: The once-a-week descent to defecate is right, but the breath-holding comparison rests on unsourced reports (up to 40 minutes, sometimes 'over 20') against a rough dolphin average of about 10 minutes, and dolphin species vary; it is stated as firmer fact than the evidence supports.
checks.fix: It climbs down from the treetops only about once a week — to relieve itself — and is reported to hold its breath underwater for up to 40 minutes.

checks.text: This famously slow-moving Central and South American mammal dangles upside down from branches by long, curved claws.
checks.evidence: Found in tropical rainforests of Central and South America; long curved claws let them hang upside down from branches. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sloth

checks.text: About 2% of people are born with Meckel's diverticulum, a pouch on this organ left over from the embryo's yolk stalk, which medical students remember by a 'rule of twos'.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: present in about 2% of the population, in the distal ileum, 'a vestigial remnant of the vitelline duct' linking the midgut to the yolk sac, remembered by 'the rule of 2s' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meckel%27s_diverticulum

checks.text: A 2014 Swedish study found the gut's inner lining covers about 30 to 40 m², nearer half a badminton court than the oft-quoted tennis court, and most of that lies in this organ.
checks.evidence: ScienceNordic (Apr 2014): Gothenburg (Sahlgrenska) researchers found 30 to 40 m², 'half a badminton court rather than a tennis court' https://www.sciencenordic.com/forskningno-gut-human-body/guts-match-the-surface-area-of-a-studio-apartment/1400373 ; BioNumbers (Helander & Fändriks 2014): total ~32 m², of which small intestine 30 m² https://bionumbers.hms.harvard.edu/bionumber.aspx?id=111126

checks.text: The middle section of this organ, the jejunum, is named from the Latin for 'fasting' because anatomists usually found it empty after death; the word 'jejune' shares the root.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: the jejunum is the second part of the small intestine (between duodenum and ileum), from Latin jejunus 'fasting', because it was 'frequently found to be void of food following death'; 'jejune' comes from the same root https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jejunum

checks.text: This coiled tube between the stomach and the colon, lined with millions of finger-like villi, is where most of the nutrients from our food are absorbed.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: 'It lies between the stomach and large intestine'; 'the site where most of the nutrients from ingested food are absorbed'; lined with 'small finger-like protrusions called intestinal villi' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Small_intestine

checks.text: This animal can seal itself in and sleep through dry spells; one glued to a card at the British Museum in 1846 woke up about four years later.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: a specimen was 'glued to an index card at the British Museum in March 1846' and found alive in March 1850. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eremina_desertorum

checks.text: Its tongue is a ribbon set with up to 25,000 tiny teeth, and most land-dwelling kinds are both male and female at once.
checks.evidence: EarthSky: land snails 'can have up to 25,000 tiny teeth' on a radula, and 'Snails are hermaphrodites'. https://earthsky.org/earth/land-snails-lifeform-of-the-week/

checks.text: It glides on a single muscular foot, and its slime lets it crawl along a razor's edge unharmed.
checks.evidence: British Wildlife (Robert Burton): 'the pinpoint sensitivity and control in the snail's foot allow it to climb over a razorblade without coming into contact with the cutting edge'. https://www.britishwildlife.com/?p=8970
checks.problem: The cited source says a snail can climb over a razor blade 'without coming into contact with the cutting edge', and credits the sensitivity and control of its foot, not its slime. 'Crawl along a razor's edge' overstates it.
checks.fix: It glides on a single muscular foot so sensitive and controlled that it can creep over a razor blade unharmed.

checks.text: This slow, shell-carrying mollusc leaves a shimmering trail and is a close cousin of the slug.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: gastropods without a conspicuous shell are called slugs; snails move on a muscular foot over a secreted mucus layer. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snail

checks.text: This app launched in 2011 under the name Picaboo, and was renamed just two months later.
checks.evidence: Launched as Picaboo on iOS on July 8, 2011; relaunched as Snapchat in September 2011. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snapchat

checks.text: This app's original idea came from Stanford student Reggie Brown, who was pushed out months after launch and settled with its founders for $157.5 million in 2014.
checks.evidence: Former Stanford student Reggie Brown brought the disappearing-pictures idea to Spiegel, was ousted months after launch, and settled with Spiegel and Murphy for $157.5 million in September 2014. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snapchat

checks.text: In 2013, this app's 23-year-old co-founder turned down a $3 billion cash offer from Facebook.
checks.evidence: WSJ (Nov 2013) reported Snapchat spurned an all-cash Facebook offer of $3 billion or more; Spiegel was 23. https://slate.com/technology/2013/11/facebook-offered-3-billion-for-snapchat-evan-spiegel-said-no.html ; all-cash detail via https://www.csmonitor.com/layout/set/amphtml/Technology/Horizons/2013/1116/Why-did-Snapchat-s-23-year-old-CEO-reject-a-3-billion-buyout-offer

checks.text: Teens keep 'streaks' going by sending a daily photo on this ghost-logo app.
checks.evidence: Snapstreaks count consecutive days two users have snapped each other and are lost if both do not send a Snap within 24 hours; the ghost mascot is kept in the logo. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snapchat

snow-white-and-the-seven-dwarfs.answer: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs

checks.text: The woman who voiced this 1937 film's heroine was paid $970 in all; two years later she spoke a single line in 'The Wizard of Oz': 'Wherefore art thou Romeo?'
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: Caselotti was paid $970 in total for the film; in The Wizard of Oz (1939) she voiced the line 'Wherefore art thou Romeo?' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriana_Caselotti

checks.text: Walt Disney's honorary Oscar for this film was one full-size statuette standing above a row of miniature ones, presented to him by 10-year-old Shirley Temple.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: Disney's honorary award was one full-size statuette and seven miniatures, presented by Shirley Temple, who was 10. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snow_White_and_the_Seven_Dwarfs_(1937_film)

checks.text: Names considered for the little men in this film included Burpy, Tubby, Shifty, Weepy and Awful, before Walt Disney settled on the final line-up.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia lists rejected names including Awful, Burpy and Tubby; Cartoon Research lists proposed names including Shifty, Burpy and Weepy. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snow_White_and_the_Seven_Dwarfs_(1937_film) https://cartoonresearch.com/index.php/seven-secrets-of-the-seven-dwarfs/

checks.text: Mocked as 'Disney's Folly' during production, this first Disney animated feature has a princess hide from her jealous stepmother with Doc, Grumpy, Sneezy, Dopey and the rest.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: industry insiders called it 'Disney's Folly' during production; it was Disney's first feature-length film. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snow_White_and_the_Seven_Dwarfs_(1937_film)

checks.text: Johannes Kepler, too short of money to buy his patron a present, wrote him a 1611 treatise on this tiny natural object as a New Year's gift about 'nothing'.
checks.evidence: St Edmund Hall blog: New Year's gift to 'his friend and patron, Wacker von Wackfels'; his salary often went unpaid, so he had nothing to give; pun on 'nichts' (nothing) and 'nix' (snow). https://www.seh.ox.ac.uk/blog/johannes-kepler-on-snowflakes

checks.text: Guinness lists the largest ones ever recorded as those that fell at Fort Keogh, Montana, in January 1887, claimed to be 15 inches wide.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: Guinness 'lists the world's largest aggregated snowflakes as those of January 1887 at Fort Keogh, Montana', 'claimed to be 38 cm (15 inches) wide'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snowflake

checks.text: A Vermont farmer took the first photograph of one through a microscope in 1885, and went on to photograph more than 5,000 of them.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: Bentley photographed snowflakes with a microscope from 1885 onward. Guinness record page cited by the writer is titled first photograph of a snowflake (Bentley, 1885); 'more than 5,000' matches the commonly cited total (about 5,000-5,381). https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/606626-first-photograph-of-a-snowflake

checks.text: These six-sided ice crystals drift down from winter clouds, and it is said that no two of them are ever exactly alike.
checks.evidence: General description; 'it is said' hedges the no-two-alike claim. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snowflake

checks.text: This sport's modern rules were first agreed in 1863 over six meetings at a London pub, the Freemasons' Tavern.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: six meetings at the Freemasons' Tavern between 26 October and December 1863 drafted the Laws of the Game. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Football_Association

checks.text: The name Americans use for this sport began as English student slang in the 1880s, a clipped form of 'association.'
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: 'soccer' arose in English public schools and universities in the 1880s as slang from 'association'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Names_for_association_football

checks.text: This sport's color-coded penalty cards were inspired by traffic lights an English referee saw while driving through London, and debuted in 1970.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: Aston got the idea at a traffic light on Kensington High Street while driving from Wembley; cards first used at the 1970 World Cup. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Aston

checks.text: In this global game, fans roar as the ball is kicked into a net; Pelé and Messi are among its legends.
checks.evidence: General description of the sport. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Football_Association

checks.text: This sky event halted a battle between the Medes and Lydians, according to Herodotus; the battle is usually dated to 585 BC.
checks.evidence: Herodotus says day turned to night during a Medes-Lydians battle and both sides stopped fighting; the eclipse is usually dated 28 May 585 BC, though some scholars dispute it. The clue's 'usually dated' covers this. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eclipse_of_Thales

checks.text: During one of these in 1919, Arthur Eddington photographed stars near the Sun to test Einstein's prediction that gravity bends light.
checks.evidence: ESA: the 1919 eclipse expeditions led by Eddington photographed stars near the Sun in Brazil and Principe to test Einstein's light-bending prediction. https://www.esa.int/Science_Exploration/Space_Science/Relativity_and_the_1919_eclipse

checks.text: The total phase of this event can never last longer than about seven and a half minutes.
checks.evidence: Guinness: 'The maximum possible duration of an eclipse of the Sun is 7min 31sec.' https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/65009-longest-total-solar-eclipse

checks.text: Safe-viewing glasses are a must for this event, when the Moon blots out the Sun.
checks.evidence: General knowledge: the Moon passes in front of the Sun, and eye protection is needed. ESA's eclipse page describes the Moon covering the Sun. https://www.esa.int/Science_Exploration/Space_Science/Relativity_and_the_1919_eclipse

checks.text: In 1709 the Upminster rector William Derham published the first fairly accurate figure for how fast this travels: 1,072 Paris feet per second.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: Derham, rector of Upminster 1689-1735, published in 1709 a more accurate speed of sound of about 1,072 Parisian feet per second, observed from the tower of St Laurence, Upminster. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Derham

checks.text: This travels more than four times faster through fresh water than through air, and almost 15 times faster through iron.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: in fresh water (1481 m/s) sound is 'slightly more than 4.3 times as fast' as in air (343 m/s), and in iron (5120 m/s) 'almost 15 times as fast'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speed_of_sound

checks.text: The 1883 eruption of Krakatoa made the loudest one of these in recorded history, heard on an island nearly 3,000 miles away.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: the third explosion on 27 August 1883 was 'the loudest-known sound in history' and was heard on Rodrigues, about 4,800 km (3,000 mi) away. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1883_eruption_of_Krakatoa

checks.text: This is what your ears pick up — from a whisper to a thunderclap — as vibrations move through the air.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: sound is audible vibration that travels as pressure waves through a medium such as air, and the sensation the ear produces from them. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound

checks.text: This physical constant was first shown to have a measurable value in 1676, when Danish astronomer Ole Rømer timed the eclipses of Jupiter's moon Io.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: in 1676 Danish astronomer Ole Rømer, timing eclipses of Io, demonstrated that light has a measurable speed. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R%C3%B8mer's_determination_of_the_speed_of_light

checks.text: Since 1983 its value has been fixed exactly by definition, and the meter itself is now defined by it.
checks.evidence: NIST: in 1983 the meter was redefined by light's travel time, fixing c at exactly 299,792,458 m/s. https://www.nist.gov/si-redefinition/meter

checks.text: Computer pioneer Grace Hopper handed out pieces of wire just under a foot long to show the farthest a signal can go in a nanosecond, a limit set by this constant.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: Hopper handed out wires 11.8 inches (30 cm) long, the distance light travels in a nanosecond, noting it is the maximum distance a signal can travel. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grace_Hopper

checks.text: Physicists label this constant, about 300,000 kilometers per second, with the letter c.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: symbol c, value 299,792.458 km/s, about 300,000 km/s. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speed_of_light

checks.text: This creature can't chew, so it coats or fills its prey with digestive juices and then sucks up the liquefied remains.
checks.evidence: SEDL: spiders don't chew; they inject digestive enzymes that liquefy the prey's tissues and then pump out the liquid. (Some spiders also regurgitate fluid onto prey, which 'coats' covers.) https://sedl.org/scimath/pasopartners/spiders/lesson3a1.html

checks.text: In 1832, thousands of these tiny creatures drifted on the wind onto Darwin's ship, HMS Beagle, about 60 miles off the coast of Argentina.
checks.evidence: Darwin's diary: sailing between Monte Video and Buenos Ayres, spiders traveled 'at least 60 miles from the Northern shore', 'some thousands in the ship'; Journal: 'within the mouth of the Plata ... distant 60 miles from land'. https://darwin-online.org.uk/converted/manuscripts/Darwin_C_R_CUL-DAR30.117-119.html https://darwin-online.org.uk/converted/published/1873_Aeronaut_F1765.html
checks.problem: Darwin's zoological diary (31 Oct 1832) places the Beagle in the Río de la Plata between Montevideo and Buenos Aires and says the spiders came at least 60 miles from the northern shore, which is Uruguay, not Argentina. 'Off the coast of Argentina' is not supported; the 60 miles and 'some thousands' are.
checks.fix: In 1832, thousands of these tiny creatures drifted on the wind onto Darwin's ship, HMS Beagle, about 60 miles from land at the mouth of the Río de la Plata.

checks.text: One kind of this creature, the bolas, swings a line tipped with a sticky glob at moths it has lured in by copying a female moth's scent.
checks.evidence: University of Kentucky (Haynes): adult female bolas spiders release chemicals mimicking moth sex pheromones and strike approaching male moths with a sticky ball at the end of a short thread swung with a foreleg. http://www.uky.edu/Ag/Entomology/entdept/faculty/khaynes/haynesr3.html

checks.text: This web-spinning creepy-crawly snares flies in silk and stars in many a Halloween decoration.
checks.evidence: General description; spiders capture insect prey with silk (bolas line described as a highly reduced web). http://www.uky.edu/Ag/Entomology/entdept/faculty/khaynes/haynesr3.html

checks.text: This superhero debuted in 1962 in the last issue of 'Amazing Fantasy,' a comic already due to be cancelled.
checks.evidence: Amazing Fantasy #15 (1962) introduced Spider-Man and 'was indeed the final issue'. Lee recalled 'the title had been slated for cancellation'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazing_Fantasy

checks.text: This superhero's 2011 Broadway musical, with songs by Bono and the Edge, cost a record $75 million.
checks.evidence: It is 'the most expensive Broadway production in history, with a budget of $75 million'. Music and lyrics are by Bono and The Edge, and it officially opened June 14, 2011. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spider-Man:_Turn_Off_the_Dark

checks.text: This superhero broke a comic-book habit of his day: he was a teenager who starred as the hero himself, not a sidekick with an adult mentor.
checks.evidence: 'Unlike previous teen heroes, Spider-Man was not a sidekick nor did he have a mentor.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spider-Man

checks.text: This red-and-blue-suited superhero, secretly Peter Parker, shoots webs from his wrists and swings between New York skyscrapers.
checks.evidence: His secret identity is Peter Parker of Queens, New York City, and he builds 'wrist-mounted web-shooter devices'. The red-and-blue suit is not stated on this page but is his standard costume. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Parker

checks.text: This organ is found in every vertebrate except lampreys and hagfish.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: 'The only vertebrates lacking a spleen are the lampreys and hagfishes.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spleen

checks.text: Indonesia's Bajau 'sea nomads', who free-dive for food, have this organ about 50 percent larger than their farming neighbors, which seems to help them stay under longer.
checks.evidence: Nat Geo: median Bajau spleen '50 percent bigger' than Saluan; link to diving is suggestive, matching 'seems to help'. https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/bajau-sea-nomads-free-diving-spleen-science

checks.text: The Talmud called this the organ of laughter, but Greek medicine said it stored black bile, which linked it to melancholy.
checks.evidence: Wikipedia: Talmud (Berachoth 61b) calls the spleen the organ of laughter; Greek humourism made it a reservoir of black bile, linked to melancholia. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spleen

checks.text: This organ in the upper left of the abdomen removes old red blood cells, and people can live without it if it ruptures and has to come out.
checks.evidence: Standard anatomy. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spleen

checks.text: This cartoon inspired a Broadway musical that earned 12 Tony nominations in 2018, tying for the most that year.
checks.evidence: The musical received 12 Tony nominations in 2018, tying Mean Girls for the most. https://playbill.com/article/2018-tony-award-nominations-spongebob-squarepants-and-mean-girls-lead-the-pack

checks.text: Ernest Borgnine and Tim Conway, co-stars of the 1960s sitcom McHale's Navy, voiced a pair of elderly superheroes on this cartoon.
checks.evidence: Borgnine voiced Mermaid Man and Conway Barnacle Boy; the two co-starred in the 1960s sitcom McHale's Navy. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mermaid_Man_and_Barnacle_Boy

checks.text: This cartoon's creator taught marine biology, and many of its characters began in a comic he drew for his students called 'The Intertidal Zone.'
checks.evidence: Hillenburg taught marine biology at the Orange County Marine Institute and made The Intertidal Zone to teach his students; many of its creatures evolved into the show's characters. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Hillenburg

checks.text: This cartoon's hero lives in a pineapple under the sea with his pet snail, Gary, on the same street as his best friend, Patrick the starfish.
checks.evidence: Squidward's moai sits between SpongeBob's pineapple and Patrick Star's rock on Conch Street; Gary the snail is SpongeBob's pet. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squidward_Tentacles

checks.text: In 1924 the champions taking this trophy to their victory party set it on a roadside curb during car trouble, drove off without it, and later found it still there.
checks.evidence: NHL.com: 1924, Dandurand's Model T stalled on a hill on the way to the celebration at his house; Cleghorn set the Cup on the curb; it was found still there about an hour later. https://nhl.com/news/stanley-cup-has-strange-and-colorful-past

checks.text: The bowl on top of this trophy originally cost ten guineas, and every 13 years the oldest band of names is removed to make room for new winners.
checks.evidence: Bowl bought for ten guineas; every 13 years, when the bottom band fills, the top (oldest) band is removed. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Cup

checks.text: Engravers have misspelled team names on this trophy, carving 'BQSTQN' for the Boston Bruins in 1972 and 'Leaes' for the Toronto Maple Leafs in 1963.
checks.evidence: 'Leaes' in 1963 and 'BQSTQN' in 1972. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Cup

checks.text: This trophy, the oldest awarded to a pro sports team in North America, goes to the NHL champions, and each winning player gets to keep it for a day.
checks.evidence: 'the oldest existing trophy to be awarded to a professional sports franchise in North America'; since 1995 each team member gets it for a day. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Cup

checks.text: This film's sound designer made its signature weapon's hum by mixing the drone of an idling film projector with the buzz of a TV set.
checks.evidence: Burtt combined the hum of movie projector motors with interference from a nearby television set picked up by an unshielded microphone. (The cited diyphotography page returned 404.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Wars_(film)

checks.text: This 1977 film opened in just 32 U.S. theaters, yet it went on to pass Jaws as the highest-grossing film of its time.
checks.evidence: It 'opened with 32 engagements on the 25th of May' (43 by the opening weekend) (https://fromscripttodvd.com/star_wars_a_day_long_remembered.htm); it went on to surpass Jaws as the highest-grossing film. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Wars_(film)

checks.text: This film's desert planet takes its name from Tataouine, a town in southern Tunisia, the country where its desert scenes were shot.
checks.evidence: Lucas 'adapted the name from a town in southern Tunisia called Tataouine'; Sidi Bouhlel footage was combined with Death Valley, California footage for the canyon scenes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tatooine). checks.fix: This film's desert planet takes its name from Tataouine, a town in southern Tunisia, the country where most of its desert scenes were shot.

checks.text: In this space adventure, farm boy Luke Skywalker learns the ways of the Force and joins Han Solo and Princess Leia against Darth Vader.

checks.text: This marine animal pushes its stomach out through its mouth and digests its prey outside its own body.

checks.text: A simple eye sits at the tip of each of its arms, and it creeps along on hundreds of little tube feet.

checks.text: This five-armed creature, often found clinging to rocks in tide pools, is shaped like the ornament on top of many Christmas trees.

checks.text: This show's tense music was built on a dissonant chord from 'Mars' in Holst's The Planets, and its pitch rose a semitone with each question.
checks.evidence: Keith Strachan Wikipedia: 'he took inspiration from a dissonant chord in "Mars" from Holst's The Planets suite.' British show Wikipedia: three variations; 'the second and third compositions focused on emphasising the increased tension', and as a contestant progressed 'the pitch of the music was increased by a semitone for each subsequent question.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Strachan https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Who_Wants_to_Be_a_Millionaire%3F_(British_game_show)
checks.problem: The pitch did not rise with every question. The Strachans wrote three variations, and only the second and third raised the pitch a semitone per question as contestants reached higher amounts. 'Built on' the Mars chord is also a little strong: the sources say the theme was inspired by it.
checks.fix: This show's tense music took its cue from a dissonant chord in 'Mars' from Holst's The Planets, and in later rounds its pitch rose a semitone with each question.

The Mississippi State invention archive quotes Bishop Milton Wright that a few weeks after the blow Wilbur 'began to be affected with nervous palpitations of the heart,' which 'precluded the realization of the former idea of his parents, of giving him a course in Yale College,' and says he stayed home for four years caring for his dying mother Susan. Two caveats that do not change the substance: the Bishop's diary calls the implement a bat (Wikipedia and most popular accounts say a hockey stick), and that archive notes he suffered 'perhaps as much from depression as from his vaguely-defined heart disorder.' The Wright Brothers Aviation Center page says Dunbar launched the paper for Dayton's African-American community in late 1890 and that it 'lasted only three issues,' which supports 'short-lived.' https://wright-brothers.org/History_Wing/Wright_Story/Career_Choices/Good_News_Bad_News/Good_News_Bad_News.htm

The only unstated nuance is that the Flyer was moved out of London for safe storage during World War II; the loan to the London museum still ran the full 20 years. https://airandspace.si.edu/stories/editorial/how-wright-flyer-got-smithsonian

checks.text: The idea of twisting a wing's tips in opposite directions to bank and turn came to one brother in 1899 as he idly flexed the long cardboard box a bicycle inner tube had come in.
checks.evidence: Two sources independent of the family and its museums support every claim. A U.S. federal courts exhibit on the Wright patent case says "The solution came unexpectedly one summer day in 1899" and "While talking with a customer in the shop, Wilbur idly played with a long, thin cardboard box for a bicycle inner tube", then "realized that this twisting effect could be used to change the angles of opposing biplane wings" (https://exhibits.nhd.uscourts.gov/47.htm). A Smithsonian education page describes the same object as "a cardboard container for a bicycle inner tube, which was empty and open at both ends", says that "While talking to a customer, he idly picked up" the box and pressed opposite corners so that "The other two corners moved simultaneously - one went up and the other went down", and dates the biplane kite built on the idea to the summer of 1899 (https://smithsonianeducation.org/educators/lesson_plans/wright/wing_warping.html). Neither page hedges the anecdote, and both are consistent with the clue on the year, the object, the idle handling and the opposite-direction twist. The only variation between retellings is minor and does not touch the clue: some accounts have a customer buying the tube while the Smithsonian page has Wilbur picking up an already empty box, and some note he had also watched buzzards twist their wing tips before this. https://smithsonianeducation.org/educators/lesson_plans/wright/wing_warping.html
